vignette: The memory begins, as it always does, with the smell of wet concrete and stale coffee. He is thirty-two again, working the night shift at a community college where he has built a quiet reputation as a reliable tutor. A student asks to stay late to review calculus. The door clicks shut behind him. He does not often speak of the hours that follow, but his hands still trace the same path along his thighs when he describes it-fingers pressing into his own jeans as if to anchor himself to the room. He remembers the coldness of the chair, the sharp metallic sound of the lock, and the way his breath catches in his throat, not from fear at first, but from the sheer, disorienting violation of a space he trusted. He does not fight. He goes rigid, a survival strategy that now sits heavy in his chest like swallowed glass. In the weeks that follow, he stops teaching. The sight of a desk chair makes his stomach turn. He takes a leave, then leaves the position entirely, taking a remote job transcribing academic papers for graduate students. It keeps him indoors, keeps him silent, keeps him from having to look anyone in the eye. He does not date. He stops returning phone calls from old friends. At fifty-seven, he lives in a ground-floor apartment with the curtains drawn most of the day. The silence, he thinks, is safer than surprise. He wakes before his alarm. Again. Every morning, his body arrives first: heart hammering against his ribs, muscles coiled, breath shallow. He checks the door lock twice, then a third time, running his palm over the deadbolt until the metal warms under his skin. When he finally rises, he moves through his kitchen like a man walking through a room full of broken glass. He makes tea, sets it aside, watches it cool. His mind drifts to the last time he sat in a classroom, the way a student's knee brushed his own, the sudden, suffocating wave of nausea. He pushes the memory down with a textbook, a spreadsheet, anything that demands linear focus. Tutoring returns when his savings dwindle, but he adapts it to fit his limits. He teaches online now, video off, audio only. He keeps his hands visible at the bottom of the screen, pacing his own desk to avoid sitting too long. His students know him as thorough, slightly distant, unyielding on deadlines. They do not notice how he flinches when the call connects, or how he times his sessions to end exactly at the hour, never a minute longer. He tells himself it is professionalism. He knows, in the quiet moments, that it is perimeter checking. Some evenings, the intrusion comes unbidden. A siren outside, a heavy footstep in the hallway, the wrong tone in a colleague's voice-all of it can spike his pulse into his ears. He will step outside then, into the cool air, and press his palms flat against the brick wall until the ringing in his head subsides. He does not cry. He has not cried since the hospital. He just stands there, counting the bricks, grounding himself in the physical world while the past bleeds through the cracks of the present. He sits across from me now, shoulders rounded forward, eyes fixed on the space between his knees. His breathing is steady, but his right leg bounces beneath the desk, a metronome keeping time with something he cannot name. He speaks in careful, measured sentences, choosing each word like a stone dropped into still water. He says he is tired, not of the work, but of the watchfulness. He says he knows he should feel differently, that the world did not end on that night, that he is still here, still breathing, still showing up. He says it all without looking up. The chair is empty. The door is locked. He waits for the next hour to pass.
